           (3) The specific financial requirements needed to support the company’s base-case operating
               plan are determined. This information is obtained from the pro forma statements.
           (4) The specific sources of capital that will be used to meet the financial requirements are identified.
           (5) The initially projected financial statements are then modified to include the addition of the
               capital needed to finance the projected assets. This involves adjusting the pro forma income
               statement to include the interest charges associated with any additional debt and an adjust-




                                                                                                                     SE
               ment to dividends paid if new stock must be issued. These modifications change the initially
               projected retained earnings and thus change the “external funds needed” to finance the asset




                                                                                                                    U
               expansion. These feedback effects require the use of an iterative process to produce a consis-




                                                                                                       M
               tent final set of financial statements. In the past, all this has been done manually—which
               takes a good bit of time—but Brent has been working to develop a computerized model to




                                                                                                      O
               speed up the process.




                                                                                                     O
                                                                                                    R
                 ABM’s 1988 through 1992 historical financial statements, along with three key ratios and




                                                                                              SS
          industry averages, are given in Tables 1 and 2. The company was operating its fixed assets at full
          capacity in 1992, so its $59.15 million in sales represented full-capacity sales. Since the firm’s




                                                                                        LA
          marketing department is forecasting a 20 percent increase in sales for 1993, new assets will have to
          be added. For planning purposes, Brent assumes (1) that accounts payable and accruals will spon-




                                                                                     C
          taneously increase in accordance with standard industry practices, (2) that new long-term capital will




                                                                                R
          be raised in accordance with the firm’s target capitalization ratios which call for 20 percent long-term




                                                                             O
          debt and 80 percent common equity (measured at market value), and (3) that short-term bank loans,
          reported as notes payable, will be assumed to grow along with sales, since they are used to finance
                                                                      LE
          the firm’s working capital needs. (Note that new common equity includes both new retained earn-
                                                                 SA
          ings and new common stock sales.)
                 ABM currently has 4 million shares of common stock outstanding, and the market price is
          $6. The dividend in 1992 was $0.25 per share, and management does not intend to increase the per
                                                             R



          share dividend in 1993. New long-term debt would carry a 12.0 percent coupon, and it would be
                                                      FO




          issued at par. New short-term debt will cost 10.0 percent. The firm’s combined federal and state tax
          rate is 40 percent.
                                                  T




                 ABM’s senior managers go off on a one week retreat each November to work on the five-
                                              O




          year plan and the budget for the coming year. Prior to the retreat, the various division managers must
                                           N




          prepare reports which the top executives will review beforehand and then discuss at the retreat. As
          financial manager, Brent normally prepares some first approximation financial forecasts which are
                                      −




          then modified during the retreat as a result of strategic decisions made at that time. The modified
                               LY




          statements are used to show the financial implications of different operating plans. However, Brent
          recently underwent a difficult ulcer operation and, because of a slow recovery, he will neither be able
                           N




          to attend the retreat, nor to prepare the background report for it. Therefore, his assistant, ready or not,
                        O




          must assume his duties.
                  W




                 Even though he could not get out of bed, Brent called his assistant to the hospital, and they dis-
            IE




          cussed what needed to be done. First, Brent told his assistant he had almost finished a computer-
          ized model that would aid in the process. Brent also indicated that the model needed to be debugged,
          EV




          or at least checked out, by first making “by-hand” projections and then seeing if the model generated
          the same set of data. If a discrepancy is discovered, it will be necessary to find out where the error
      R




          lies. Brent also cautioned his assistant that it would be necessary to explain to the executives how any
      R




          changes in operating conditions would affect the external funds requirement, as well as how any
 FO




          changes in the financing mix would affect everything, including external funding requirements, earn-
          ings per share, and the stock price. In particular, Brent warned the assistant not to try to defend the
          inputs to the forecasting process; rather, the critical thing is to be able to make adjustments in the
          likely event that the senior executives don’t like all the assumptions used in the forecast. As Brent
          pointed out, “It’s top management’s job to understand the business and to make the final assumptions
          used in the forecast and the budget. It’s our job to tell them how those assumptions interact and what




          Copyright © 1994 South-Western. All rights reserved.
                                                            Case 38 - Non-Directed - Financial Forecasting              821
                                                                                Case: 38 Financial Forecasting


     the final outcome will be if their assumptions hold true. We ought to use reasonable inputs for our
     report and basic forecasts, but our real job in the planning process is to show top management what
     will happen under different operating conditions.”
            Assume that you are Brent’s assistant and that you must take his place at the retreat. Know-
     ing the anxiety you must feel, Brent left the following memo containing some suggestions which
     might be helpful:




                                                                                                                   SE
           Not all of the managers feel comfortable using only one method to calculate ABM’s EFN for
           1993. Thus, forecast the firm’s financial statements and EFN for 1993 using the proportional




                                                                                                                  U
           growth (percentage of sales) method. However, be aware that Daniel Hays, vice president of




                                                                                                    M
           accounting, also likes EFN determined by using the following formula.




                                                                                                   O
                   External             Required           Spontaneous          Increase in




                                                                                                  O
                     funds      =      increase in –        increase in     –    retained
                    needed               assets              liabilities         earnings




                                                                                                 R
                                                                                           SS
                     EFN         =        (A/S)D S      –       (L/S)D S          – MS1(1 – d).




                                                                                    LA
           Here,
           A/S =        Assets/Sales = required dollar increase in assets per $1 increase in sales




                                                                                 C
           L/S =        Spontaneous liabilities/Sales = spontaneously generated financing per $1




                                                                            R
                        increase in sales




                                                                        O
           S1    =      Total sales projected for next year (S0 = last year’s sales)
           DS    =      Change in sales = S1 – S0                LE
           M     =      Profit margin
                                                            SA
           d     =      Dividend payout ratio

     Many of the executives at the retreat will not understand the assumptions implied in the percentage
                                                      R



     of sales method or will at least be concerned with their validity. In addition, before you leave for
                                                FO




     the retreat, run a regression of total assets on sales to test one of the assumptions. Lastly, although
     I’m not sure if the senior executives would be interested in this information, you might want to cal-
                                            T




     culate the firm’s current ratio, profit margin, ROE, and EPS for 1992 and 1993 and discuss how the
                                        O




     projected ratios would change as such things as the sales growth rate, the payout ratio, the capital
                                     N




     structure, and the profit margin change.
                                                                                              Good luck!
                                 −




                                                                                              Brent
                          LY




     While at the retreat and discussing the forecast with ABM’s senior executives, the vice president
     for manufacturing informs the group that preliminary studies indicate that fixed assets were actu-
                      N




     ally being operated at only 80 or 90 percent of capacity in 1992. The other executives become imme-
                   O




     diately concerned as to how projected external capital requirements for 1993 will be affected.
             W




     Fortunately, you brought your laptop as well as a backup along on the retreat.
       IE




           Also, being the accounting whiz that he is, Daniel Hays notices that according to the 1992 bal-
     ance sheet, the firm’s capitalization ratio and total-debt-to-total-assets ratio are both higher than the
     EV




     firm’s target capital structure. In fact, he states that “the capital structure is seriously out of balance
     and the company is using far too much debt. I believe we should modify the mix of debt and equity
     R




     used in the forecasts.” You get a lump in your throat as everyone at the retreat immediately looks
 R




     to you. “Well, what do you think,” asks Bill Herbert Walker Clinton, chairman of the board, in a
FO




     gruff voice.
           Finally, one of the executives asks what can be done with the excess funds that are fore-
     casted to be generated in 1993, if any exist.
